title: GPX Elevation Loss Calculator: Total Descent
description: Sum the negative elevation changes in a GPX track with the GPX Elevation Loss Calculator — total descent from the recording. Free, in-browser.
summary_sentence: For example, the profile 100 → 112 → 108 → 125 → 121 → 140 metres loses only 8 metres — the two small dips of 4 metres each — while gaining 48.

examples.label: Example · The sum, step by step

body.t: Elevations 100, 112, 108, 125, 121, 140: drops are −4 and −4, so loss = 8 m, while rises total 48 m. Gain − loss = +40 m = last minus first elevation — the identity every profile must satisfy, and a one-line audit of any platform's numbers.

Start at a 2,400 m pass, finish at a 900 m village with two 150 m re-climbs between: loss = (2,400 − 900) + 300 = 1,800 m. The descents include re-descending every re-climb — loss counts ground, not intentions.

popular_table.title: Loss, gain and net — the identity
popular_table.intro: Three measures, one equation that must always hold: gain − loss = net change.
popular_table.note: Platforms that threshold small changes lower both gain and loss together; the identity survives only if their filtering is symmetric. A broken identity is a fingerprint of one-sided processing.

faq: Why is loss not just start minus finish?
Because terrain undulates: every dip after a rise adds descent the endpoints never confess. Endpoint subtraction gives net change; loss is the accumulated downhill you actually travelled.
Does it smooth the elevation first?

The sum runs over the recorded steps as they stand. GPS altitude jitter adds phantom descents on flat ground — platforms threshold them away, which is why their loss figures sit below a raw sum like this one.
They contribute no step, and sparse elevation understates loss. The honest reading notes how many points carried elevation at all.
Both — descents are quoted in feet by American skiers and metres by European ones, and the converter's convention covers both audiences.
Barometric series descend more smoothly; GPS altitude jitters, manufacturing small false losses on the flat. The file's source explains its own bias.
Loops must have loss equal to gain?
Within noise, yes — a closed loop returns to its start elevation, so gain − loss ≈ 0. A big mismatch is altitude noise confessing itself.
